strengths: The paper identifies and clearly motivates a real, well-documented failure mode (mean-collapse) in perturbation-response prediction, framing it both conceptually (Fig. 1) and mathematically (decomposition of MSE loss in Sec. 3.1), which gives a crisp explanation for why naive reconstruction objectives underperform on DEGs.

The proposed method combines an interpretable set of components (perturbation-conditioned subgraph extraction via semantic+structural node scoring with Gumbel-Softmax sampling, Huber-based non-DEG suppression, and a DEG-alignment loss) that directly target the diagnosed failure mode rather than being generic architectural tweaks.

The empirical evaluation is unusually extensive for a method paper: four cell lines, an independent 'Systema' evaluation protocol, cross-cell-line generalization, DEG-threshold sensitivity analysis, KG-source/density ablations, attention-threshold ablations, effect-size stratification, and pathway-level (GSEA) case studies, which substantially strengthens robustness claims.

Consistent improvements are shown across nearly all baselines and metrics, with particularly notable and biologically meaningful gains on DEG-aware metrics and for small/medium effect-size perturbations, directly supporting the central mean-collapse narrative.

The ablations (Fig. 4, 5, 20-24) are thoughtful and isolate the contributions of zcontext and Lnon, and the KG-density/source study yields a genuinely useful empirical insight (coverage + moderate sparsity beats larger, denser graphs) relevant beyond this paper.
weaknesses: Improvements over the strongest baseline (TxPert) on the primary Pearson-Δ/PDS metrics are often modest (a few percentage points, Table 1), and no statistical significance testing (e.g., paired tests, confidence intervals, multiple seeds/runs) is reported to establish that gains are not within noise, despite reporting std across perturbations.

The cross-cell-line generalization result (Table 13, Fig. 13) shows a simple 'Perturb Mean' baseline outperforms all learned methods including ADAPERT on Pearson-Δ, and ADAPERT is only best 'among deep-learning models'—this somewhat undercuts the generality claim and is not sufficiently discussed as a limitation in the main text.

Several key implementation details are only in the appendix or missing from the main text (e.g., exact architecture sizes, hyperparameter search protocol for λ_non/λ_align, number of training seeds/runs, threshold T selection procedure beyond a small sweep), which affects reproducibility of the reported numbers.

The method relies on LLM-generated/NCBI textual descriptions and OpenAI embeddings for semantic scoring, introducing a potentially costly, non-fully-reproducible, and version-dependent dependency (GPT-4o, proprietary embedding API) that is not deeply analyzed for its own contribution vs. the structural GNN pathway (no ablation strictly isolating text-embedding contribution vs. graph structure alone).

DEG identification (used both for training supervision via Lnon/Lalign and for evaluation) is derived from the same statistical procedure, raising a potential circularity/leakage concern between the training signal and DEG-aware evaluation metrics; the appendix sensitivity analysis (App. D) addresses threshold choice but does not fully rule out the more fundamental concern that DEG-based training could inflate DEG-based metrics relative to baselines not given DEG-aware supervision.

The presentation of the appendix is very large and somewhat redundant (multiple overlapping figures/tables reporting similar comparisons under slightly different protocols), which could be tightened; some claims like '28% improvement' in the abstract are based on a single Table 3 stratification without broader corroboration in the main text.
